doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Eye-rolling at 'America's only art form' and 'classical music'
summary: He objects to the clichés that jazz is America's only original art form, its classical music, or once its popular music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: When you transcribe this you can transcribe that I’m going to roll my eyes.
Okay. Well I’m rolling mine too and I’m off camera.
What about the blues? Isn’t the blues its own original American art form?
Okay. Why did you roll your eyes?

Because there’s two things that I roll my eyes at, and I roll them in great respect. I mean, and he did roll his eyes, that those kind of statements I don’t know how much good they do. I don’t know how much light they shed on anything, because well what about cartoons? What about a certain kind of cinema? What about any number of things that are uniquely American. I mean early on Albert Murray had me read a book called American Humor by Constance Rourke, it was written back around 1930 or so. And you start to see all these various components of so many different things that are part Native American © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

and part African-American and part Yankee and part Dutch and part Asian and all these kind of things. And you start to realize early on that the one and only kind of thing doesn’t really work. And the other statement that we can just get it out of the way that I also really roll my eyes at is that jazz is America’s classical music, and also jazz was America’s popular music at one time, which it never was. So those are the three oft- repeated canards, moldy canards that kind of get me going you know. But yeah.
Now I can use it. Hey next time you see Loren, want to see him roll his eyes? Just try this one on him.
And you can take that little video clip of me and just loop it.

Yeah the first time I saw jazz is America’s classical music was in the context of another person saying, “Please, let’s not call it that. Do you want it to be treated like classical music is treated?” Do you want it to be shown only — I mean the whole routine.

Yeah. And let’s not forget you know that Ellington and Dizzy Gillespie and Max Roach and Fletcher and many other people wanted to get rid of the word “jazz” early on. But that’s not so much about my biography. But, but these are important things to talk about. I mean frankly, Monk, I mean if this was another context I would love to interview — right now I’m kind of dying to know what you think about all these things. No, but I mean it. I’m serious. Because you’ve taught and you’ve been around for a long time and have the benefit of this incredible archive of interviews that I haven’t said, I’m proud to be asked to be a member of. And I’m not being unctuous here. I’ve spent quite a bit of time watching them. I will look at them for a while then I’ll go back and go oh my God look at this and I’ll look at one that I didn’t want to look at another time. And I’ve learned a lot from them. So I would love to hear your take on all this stuff too.
